i-4.4-manage-knowledge.title: 4.4 Manage Project Knowledge: tacit vs explicit knowledge, knowledge and information management, lessons learned register
i-4.4-manage-knowledge.notes: Use existing knowledge and create new knowledge to achieve objectives and contribute to organisational learning; key benefits: prior knowledge is leveraged and project knowledge is available to operations and future projects; performed throughout. Explicit knowledge can be codified in words, pictures, numbers; tacit knowledge is personal and hard to express (beliefs, insights, experience, know-how). Knowledge management has two purposes - reuse existing and create new knowledge - underpinned by knowledge sharing and knowledge integration. Misconceptions: that it is just documenting knowledge, or just collecting lessons learned at the end. Codified explicit knowledge lacks context and is open to interpretation; tacit knowledge carries context but is shared through conversation and interaction. The most important part is creating an atmosphere of trust so people are motivated to share; tools fail without motivation. Practice mixes knowledge management (people interacting) and information management (codifying explicit knowledge). Inputs: plan (all components); documents (lessons learned register, project team assignments, RBS, source selection criteria, stakeholder register - to see what knowledge exists and is missing); deliverables; EEFs (trusting, no-blame culture and value placed on learning; geographic distribution; knowledge experts; legal/confidentiality); OPAs (policies on confidentiality, security, retention, copyright, classified information, metadata, authorised technology and social media; personnel administration and competency frameworks; communication requirements - formal communication suits sharing information, informal communication is better for creating new knowledge and integrating across diverse groups; formal learning reviews before, during and after). Tools: expert judgment; knowledge management (networking incl. online forums, communities of practice and special interest groups, meetings incl. virtual, work shadowing and reverse shadowing, discussion forums, seminars and conferences, workshops and learning reviews, storytelling, creativity and ideas management, knowledge fairs and cafes, interactive training; face-to-face builds trust best, virtual maintains it; choice depends on innovation, complexity and team diversity); information management (codifying lessons, lessons learned register, library services, information gathering, PMIS with document management; enhance with a 'contact me' function); interpersonal skills (active listening, facilitation, leadership, networking, political awareness). Outputs: lessons learned register (category, description, impact, recommendations, proposed actions; challenges, problems, realised risks and opportunities; created early in this process and then updated by many processes; can include video, pictures, audio; at end of project or phase transferred to the lessons learned repository, an OPA); plan updates; OPA updates (new knowledge codified or embedded in deliverables and improved processes).

i-4.5-monitor-control-work.title: 4.5 Monitor and Control Project Work: integrated monitoring, data analysis techniques, work performance reports
i-4.5-monitor-control-work.notes: Track, review and report overall progress against plan performance objectives; key benefits: stakeholders understand current state, actions taken and forecasts of cost and schedule; performed throughout. Monitoring = collecting, measuring and assessing measurements and trends to improve processes; control = determining corrective or preventive actions or replanning and following up. Concerns: compare actual to plan; assess periodically and recommend corrective/preventive action; check individual risk status; keep an accurate information base on products and documentation; support status reporting, progress measurement and forecasting; forecasts for current cost and schedule; monitor implementation of approved changes; report to program management; keep aligned with business needs. Inputs: plan (any component); documents (assumption log, basis of estimates, cost forecasts, issue log, lessons learned register, milestone list, quality reports, risk register, risk report, schedule forecasts); work performance information (WPD compared with plan components, documents and variables, using metrics defined at the start - e.g., money spent is meaningful only against budget, work performed, resources used and funding schedule; compare with variance thresholds to decide on preventive or corrective action); agreements (oversee contractor work); EEFs (PMIS, infrastructure, stakeholder expectations and risk thresholds, standards); OPAs (policies, financial controls, monitoring and reporting methods, issue and defect procedures, knowledge base). Tools: expert judgment (EVA, data interpretation, estimating, trend analysis, technical, risk, contract management); data analysis - alternatives analysis (choose corrective or combined actions), cost-benefit analysis (cheapest effective corrective action), earned value analysis (integrated scope, schedule, cost view), root cause analysis (main reasons for a deviation), trend analysis (forecast future performance from past results, warn early of slippage, supports preventive action), variance analysis (planned vs actual; here from an integrated perspective across cost, time, technical and resource variances); decision making (voting - unanimity, majority, plurality); meetings (face-to-face, virtual, formal, informal; user groups, review meetings). Outputs: work performance reports (status and progress reports, EV graphs, trend lines and forecasts, reserve burndown charts, defect histograms, contract performance, risk summaries; dashboards, heat reports, stop-light charts; circulated via the communications plan); change requests (expand, adjust or reduce project scope, product scope, quality requirements, schedule or cost baselines; corrective, preventive, defect repair); plan updates; document updates (cost forecasts, issue log, lessons learned register, risk register, schedule forecasts). Data flow: receives WPI from all control processes (5.5, 5.6, 6.6, 7.4, 8.3, 9.6, 10.3, 11.7, 12.3, 13.4); sends WPR to 4.6, 9.5 Manage Team, 10.2 Manage Communications, 11.7 Monitor Risks.

i-4.6-integrated-change-control.title: 4.6 Perform Integrated Change Control: CCB, configuration vs change control, decisions and the change log
i-4.6-integrated-change-control.notes: Review all change requests; approve and manage changes to deliverables, project documents and the plan; communicate decisions. Key benefit: changes considered in an integrated way addressing overall project risk (which often comes from changes made without regard to overall objectives). Performed start to finish; ultimate responsibility of the PM. Changes may affect project and product scope, any plan component or document; any stakeholder may request at any time; level of control depends on application area, complexity, contract and context. Before baselines exist, formal change control is not required; once baselined, change requests go through 4.6. The configuration management plan defines which artefacts are under configuration control; any change to a configuration element needs a change request. Verbal changes must be recorded in writing in the change/configuration management system. Requests may need schedule and cost impact estimates. Any change that may affect a baseline always requires the formal integrated process. Every documented change request is approved, deferred or rejected by a responsible individual (usually sponsor or PM, named in the plan or procedures). A CCB is a formally chartered group responsible for reviewing, evaluating, approving, deferring or rejecting changes and recording and communicating decisions. Customer or sponsor approval may be needed after CCB approval unless they sit on the CCB. Changes that don't affect baselines (only performance against them) are usually decided by the PM; baseline-affecting changes include cost, schedule, resource and risk impacts and go to the CCB; only approved changes enter a revised baseline. Inputs: plan (change management plan - directs change control and documents CCB roles; configuration management plan - configurable items; scope, schedule and cost baselines to assess impact); documents (basis of estimates, RTM, risk report); work performance reports (resource availability, schedule and cost data, EV reports, burnup/burndown); change requests; EEFs (legal, standards, governance, contracting constraints); OPAs (change control procedures, change authorisation procedures, configuration management knowledge base). Tools: expert judgment (technical, legislation, legal and procurement, configuration management, risk); change control tools - configuration control focuses on the specification of deliverables and processes; change control on identifying, documenting, approving or rejecting changes. Configuration activities: identify configuration item; record and report configuration item status; perform configuration verification and audit. Change activities: identify, document, decide on, track changes. Data analysis (alternatives analysis; cost-benefit analysis - is the change worth its cost); decision making (voting - unanimity, majority, plurality; autocratic - one person decides for the group; multicriteria decision analysis - decision matrix against predefined criteria); meetings (change control meetings with the CCB: assess impacts on time, cost, resources, risks, discuss alternatives, communicate decisions; roles documented in the change management plan). Outputs: approved change requests (implemented via 4.3; deferred or rejected ones communicated to the requester); plan updates (baselines changed only from the last baseline forward - past performance is never changed); document updates (change log records disposition of all change requests). Data flow (Figure 4-13, visually verified): receives work performance reports and change requests from 4.5, and change requests from 4.3, 5.5, 5.6, 6.6, 7.4, 8.2, 8.3, 9.3, 9.4, 9.5, 9.6, 10.3, 11.5, 11.6, 11.7, 12.1, 12.2, 12.3, 13.1, 13.3, 13.4; sends approved change requests to exactly three processes - 4.3 Direct and Manage Project Work (to implement), 8.3 Control Quality (to verify implementation) and 12.3 Control Procurements (contract changes); plan updates and change log updates go to the plan and project documents.
